description: Hi! I'm Freya (Reya), and this is Cosmic Orbit. We are taking on the Space Mission Design Game challenge this year. We want to create an amazing, science-backed space game and need a diverse crew to make it happen. Looking for developers, artists, and space enthusiasts to join the team. Let's launch this project together!
summary: Cosmic Orbit is a web-based game that lets players design a complete space mission from concept to operations. Players choose a destination, select spacecraft parts while balancing mass, power, cost, and science instruments, pick a rocket, and then face random events where their choices determine success or failure. The game ends with a score, clear explanations of the trade-offs they made, and a comparison to real missions like Juno or Perseverance. It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by showing that improving one part of a mission usually creates limits somewhere else. There is rarely one perfect design. By letting players experiment and see the results of both good and bad decisions, the game makes concepts like delta-v, payload limits, and resource constraints feel concrete. We built it with React and TypeScript so the calculations stay accurate while the experience stays approachable. The goal is to help people understand real engineering trade-offs in a way that is simple, interactive, and memorable.
details:
What does it do / how does it work?
Cosmic Orbit is a web-based game that lets players design a complete space mission from start to finish. You pick a destination (Mars, Venus, Jupiter, or Saturn), choose spacecraft parts while watching mass, power, cost, and science points, select a rocket, and then face random events during operations where you make decisions. At the end you get a score and an explanation of the trade-offs you made.

Benefits / intended impact
The game shows that there is rarely one perfect design. Improving one part of a mission (like adding more science instruments) usually creates limits somewhere else (higher mass, more power draw, or higher cost). Players learn this by experimenting and seeing the results of both successful and failed missions. It makes concepts like delta-v, payload limits, and resource constraints feel concrete instead of abstract.

Tools and technologies
We built it with React and TypeScript using Vite. The simulation logic (mass, power, cost, and delta-v calculations) is written in pure TypeScript functions. Planet data and parts come from JSON files. We used NASA and Wikimedia Commons public-domain images for the destination cards. The site is deployed on GitHub Pages.

Creativity and factors we considered
We wanted the experience to feel more like a game than a calculator, so we added Oregon Trail–style events where players make choices that affect the outcome, a floating advisor character, background music with a volume control, and a comparison to real missions (like Juno or Perseverance). We also made sure harder destinations trigger more events, and that the budget and part costs feel realistic relative to each other. The team focused on making the engineering trade-offs clear and easy to understand while still being fun to play.
dataRefs: NASA Space Apps Challenge: Space Mission Design Game
